newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Oils, tropicals push CRB to four week high.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Oils, tropicals push CRB to four week high.

text.p: Surging crude oil and petroleum product futures prices and gains in coffee and cocoa prices helped push the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index (CRB) to four week highs Monday, and the index opened higher Tuesday also, ending its month long downtrend, analysts said.
Meanwhile the Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI) is at a a five month high, extending its six week rally.
"World oil prices continue to display a strong tone with no clear evidence prices have achieved a top," Merrill Lynch senior commodities analyst, William O'Neill said.
"The complex continues to display a resilient tone with product strength leading the way in both the U.S. and Europe."
The CRB Index was up 0.25 points at 248.06 early Tuesday, its highest level since September 11.
The CRB remains well off the eight year highs at 263.79 seen in April this year, but has been slowly recovering from mid-summer lows at 240.09.
New York Futures Exchange (NYFE) November CRB futures ended up 1.85 points at 245.85 Monday, testing the top of their 243-246 range of the past three weeks.

The GSCI, which has a heavy 49 percent weighting in the energy sector, was up 0.01 points early Tuesday at 211.40, after seeing an intraday high Monday at 211.52, which surpassed the mid-summer high of 211.26, taking the index to its highest level since May.
Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) October GSCI futures ended up 2.40 points at 211.10 Monday, after seeing an intraday high at 211.30, the highest level for three weeks.
After dipping mid-summer along with oil prices, the GSCI has recovered with oil prices, extending the rally since mid-1995.

New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) November heating oil prices saw fresh five year highs in overnight electronic ACCESS trade at 76.71 cents a gallon, after ending up 2.06 cents at 76.49 cents Monday, while NYMEX November gasoline saw fresh life-of-contract highs overnight at 66.90 cents a gallon, after jumping 2.71 cents Monday to 66.34 cents.

The November heating oil/crude crack spread climbed further to $6.86 a barrel Monday, up from $6.53 Friday, pulling up NYMEX November crude oil futures to a new contract high at $25.30 a barrel Monday, not far from the five year highs at $25.70 seen in April.

"Products have been leading the oil complex since last winter and we suspect they will continue to do so," O'Neill said. "We would urge against trying to pick the top of the crude oil complex on a fundamental basis and technical indicators still have a clear upside bias," he said.

U.S. distillate inventories, which include diesel fuel and heating oil, are about 17 percent below the three year average, going into the winter, with stocks in the largest heating oil market, the U.S. East Coast, about 38 percent below their three year average, analysts noted.

But steady U.S. economic growth is also pushing up transportation sector demand for diesel. For the first 270 days of 1996, distillate fuel demand is running 4.7 percent above last year, according to the U.S. Energy Department.
"We also see some modest upside potential in the tropical markets," O'Neill said.
After the market closed Monday, the CSCE reported U.S. certified coffee stocks fell by 945 60-kg bags to a new 12 year low of 30,724 bags.
New York Coffee, Cocoa and Sugar Exchange (CSCE) December coffee ended up 2.90 cents a lb Monday at 112.70 cents, after seeing a four week high intraday at 113.00 cents.
"Supporting prices was the fact that stocks remain tight and may in fact still be declining, while roasters have been buyers when prices approach $1.00 a lb," Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka said.
--New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1640.
